passage:
Yogesh: late again, eat without me
Swati: ok
(Swati stared at her husband's word 'again'. Then she opened her chat with her sister.)
Swati: he's late AGAIN
Swati: third time this week. anniversary dinner last month, Ma's birthday, now this
Nandita: did he say why?
Swati: does he ever? it's always work. I'm always the thing that can wait 😔
Nandita: maybe something came up?
Swati: something always comes up
Nandita: want me to come over?
Swati: no. I'm fine. I'll eat alone. like always
(She put the phone face down. The actual message had said nothing about her at all. It didn't matter. She had already written the rest of the story herself.)

qa.q: What three occasions does Swati list to her sister?
qa.a: Anniversary dinner last month, Ma's birthday, and now this.

qa.q: Why does Swati read 'late again' as proof she doesn't matter?
qa.a: She links it to other late nights, so old grievances turn a neutral message into a pattern in which she is always the thing that can wait.

qa.q: What question from Nandita could help Swati most, and why?
qa.a: 'Did he say why?', because it points out that Swati doesn't actually know the reason, and asking Yogesh could replace the story with facts.

qa.q: What might Yogesh have meant when he typed 'late again'?
qa.a: He may simply have been apologising for another late night in a rush; the chat never shows his reason, only Swati's reading.

grounding: A wife reads her husband's neutral late message through past late nights and makes it a pattern, attaching a story bigger than the words.

passage: The last bus from the market had already passed the Bolpur crossing when Gopika's phone lit up. Her husband, Arnab: 'Stuck at the depot. Late. Don't wait.' She put down the ladle. Her eyes went to the calendar on the wall, where she'd circled the evenings he'd been late this month: four circles, and one of them her birthday. She remembered sitting alone with a cake that night, the candles bent in the heat. Now these six words felt like the same story in a new costume: whatever he was doing mattered more. She didn't ask why he was stuck. She didn't need to; she already knew how the story ended. She covered his plate, switched off the fan and went to bed, back to the door.

qa.q: How many evenings had Gopika circled on the calendar this month?
qa.a: Four circles, and one of them her birthday.

qa.q: Why didn't Gopika ask Arnab why he was stuck?
qa.a: Old hurts, like the lonely birthday, made her feel she already knew the answer, so her story mattered more than his actual words.

qa.q: What small step could Gopika take before going to bed with her back to the door?
qa.a: She could send one question, like 'What happened at the depot?', so the neutral message gets tested against facts rather than her old story.

qa.q: What might Arnab find when he comes home, and how might he feel?
qa.a: A covered plate, a dark room and Gopika's back turned; he may feel confused and shut out if his lateness had a real reason.

grounding: In a small town a wife reads her husband's brief late message through old hurts like a lonely birthday, and the story outweighs the sentence.
